author: Maverick Avila
title: Scientists call for conservation of horseshoe crabs found in Tawi-Tawi
content:
Researchers with a horseshoe crab in the coastal waters in Tawi-Tawi. Photo courtesy of Quesie T. Omnos and Dr. Pedrosa-Gerasmio.

Residents have confirmed to Mindanao scientists the presence of horseshoe crabs in the waters of the southern Philippine island province of Tawi-Tawi. Previously, the arthropods were only found in Palawan province, but a recent study documented fishers and coastal residents accounts of two distinct horseshoe crab species with features resembling those of the tri-spine horseshoe crab (Tachypleus tridentatus) and the mangrove horseshoe crab (Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda) in the waters of Tawi-Tawi.

The tri-spine horseshoe crab is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the mangrove horseshoe crab is listed as data deficient, meaning not much is known about its conservation status.

Ivane Pedrosa-Gerasmio, the corresponding author of the study and an associate professor in marine sciences at the Mindanao State University (MSU) – Iligan Institute of Technology, said that on her visit in a market in Bongao, the capital of Tawi-Tawi, in December 2023, locals claimed of seeing horseshoe crabs.

Pedrosa-Gerasmio told Mongabay she shared the news with her student Quesie Tolero Omnos, and together they decided to investigate further with the MSU Tawi-Tawi College of Technology and Oceanography.

“I saw an opportunity to establish baseline information that could support future research and science-based conservation initiatives for horseshoe crab species,” Omnos told Mongabay.

Pedrosa-Gerasmio, Osmos and their colleagues decided to rely on the people who best know the coastal areas. The scientists talked with 142 residents across four municipalities in Tawi-Tawi about where they had seen horseshoe crabs, how frequently, what they thought of the crabs’ population changes, and how they collected and consumed the crabs. Horseshoe crabs are called “bangkas” by the locals, due to their boat-like shape.

Those interviewed had observed horseshoe crabs turn up on sandy beaches, in mangroves, among rocky coral and seagrass, and in waters 10-15 meters (32.8-49.2 feet) deep in Bongao and other coastal towns such as Simunul, Sitangkai and Panglima Sugala.

Residents and fishers told the researchers that locals capture horseshoe crabs to use in medicine to cure asthma and other illnesses, and in rituals for people possessed by bad spirits. More than half of those interviewed also thought that horseshoe crab numbers were declining, possibly due to collection for medicinal purposes, climate change and industrial pollution.

Horseshoe crabs are often referred to as “living fossils,” because they have existed for 450 million years, outlasting dinosaurs. There are just four known species of these crabs; three are found in Asia. All Asian horseshoe crab populations are declining due to threats including habitat loss in Japan, bycatch and beach litter in Indonesia, and overharvesting, pollution and coastal reclamation in China.

Omnos said conserving the two horseshoe crab species they’ve potentially documented in Tawi-Tawi is important because of their ecological significance, possible pharmaceutical applications and cultural value to the communities.

“I believe conservation should begin with sufficient scientific evidence on their occurrence, distribution, population status, and threats, which can guide local government units in developing science-based management plans,” she said. Reposted by Bulatlat

title: Baclaran vendors bear the cost of ASEAN Summit
content:
By Reachelyn Esona and Roselle Ochobillo

From bustling streets to empty sidewalks.

This may be an image of order for some, but for Baclaran street vendors, it can mean another day of uncertainty over whether they will have earnings to take home.

In the first week of November, the local government of Parañaque City ordered a clearing operation in barangay Baclaran in time for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nation (ASEAN) summit from November 15 to 17.

The Parañaque local government said that the barangay would temporarily prohibit street vendors along Roxas Boulevard, service roads, Redemptorist Road, Quirino Avenue, and beneath LRT-1 from November 2 to November 20, to clear the way for the arriving delegates.

Among those forced to leave their usual vending spots is Eduardo Bargas, 59, who’s been selling toys along Baclaran for almost 20 years to support his wife and only child. After being dislocated, he resorted to selling bottled water to earn a living despite the imposed clearing operation.

According to Bargas, they were informed about the operation as early as November 1. While larger vendors operating inside stall establishments were allowed to continue selling, ambulant vendors like him were temporarily ordered to stop their operations.

Bargas was nearly apprehended once by the authorities. Had he been caught, he said, his goods would have been confiscated. He begged the authorities not to take his items as it was all he had to live on.

Like other vendors, Bargas’s income was severely impacted by the clearing operation. He said he used to earn up to P1,000 (approximately US$ 15.63) a day before the policy was implemented. Now, he takes home only around P300 (approximately US$ 4.69).

The same concern was shared by a 50-year-old towel and sack bag vendor, Marlyn Merioles. She sells along Baclaran to sustain her elderly mother who is on maintenance medication, and her sibling who is a person with disability.

Before the clearing, Merioles was earning around P300 (approximately US$ 4.69) to P500 (approximately US$ 7.82) a day. Since the operation began, there were days she went home with empty pockets.

Merioles said she felt disheartened by the policy. Vendors, she said, are now anxious and find it difficult to sell their goods. They are constantly on their feet, keeping an eye out for patrols roaming the area. Merioles fears that she might not see them coming as her eyesight is already failing.

They were also warned that their goods would be confiscated if they were caught. Merioles said it would be a loss they could not afford because even a whole day of selling was not enough to recover the capital they had borrowed.

Merioles said it would help if the government would sustain their daily expenses. However, she said, only a few of the vendors benefitted from the financial assistance provided for the vendors.

While the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) promised P10,000 (approximately $156.35) in cash assistance to vendors affected by the clearing operations in Baclaran, some vendors said they struggled to access the financial aid because it was reportedly limited to registered voters of Baclaran.

Rochelle Maale, who has been renting a stall in Baclaran for 10 years to sell ready-to-wear clothes, was among those who did not receive the assistance because she is not a registered voter in the area.

“The distribution of funds should be balanced… What about those who have been here for a long time but didn’t get anything?”Maale retorted.

Vendors argued that the assistance should be extended to everyone affected by the clearing operations, regardless of their place of residence, since they all experienced the impact of the clearing operations.

However, for many vendors, the issue goes beyond the limited eligibility for financial assistance.

They also questioned whether the P10,000 (approximately US$ 156.35) would be enough to sustain them after nearly 20 days of restricted operations.

Maale shared that the amount was insufficient to cover their daily expenses, especially amid rising costs of goods. “Will that P10,000 even last for a few days? No, it’s still not enough. That’s why vendors are struggling to make ends meet.”

She said some vendors have resorted to taking out loans to meet their everyday needs and restore their capital.

For vendors like Maale, the struggle extends beyond the clearing operations and financial assistance. What they need is a permanent and secure space where they can sell their merchandise, earn a living, and work without the constant fear of being arrested or displaced. (AMU, RVO)

title: Groups decry abduction attempt on Lumad youth activist in Davao City
content:
Lumad youth activist Mawing Pangadas answers questions from members of the media during a candle-lighting activity at Freedom Park in Davao City on the 2nd death anniversary of New Bataan 5 on February 24, 2024. Photo from Panalipdan Youth Davao’s Facebook page

Progressive groups condemned the alleged abduction attempt on Lumad youth activist Mawing Pangadas in Davao City.

The Hands Off Mindanao Youth Activists (HOMYA) Network reported that around 10 to 12 individuals wearing all-black clothing and caps allegedly pursued the 24-year-old youth activist along Upper Madapo Hills, Barangay 8-A, on November 17 while he was on his way home.

“[They] tried to corner him and said, ‘This is him. Do not run’,” the network stated in its alert released on November 19.

Pangadas who belongs to the Indigenous Manobo reportedly was able to escape. He lost his phone and slippers and sustained injuries after he tripped and fell down during the pursuit which reportedly lasted for three hours.

The HOMYA network said that this incident reflects the continuing attacks and harassment faced by activists. “These acts of intimidation inflict serious mental, emotional, and psychological distress not only on Mawing, the direct target of these fascist attacks, but also on his family and loved ones who are forced to live under constant fear and anxiety.”

title: Lakbayan Southern Tagalog children finally released
content:
Released Lakbayani children. (Photo from Salinlahi Facebook page)

The children were denied their rights to counsel.

The 15 minors arrested in barangay Sucat, Muntinlupa City on November 15 have been released four days later (November 19).

This follows the order issued by the Muntinlupa City Office of the Prosecutor on November 18 for the release of all those arrested.

The minors aged 14 to 17 were part of the Lakbayan Southern Tagalog that started their march from the University of the Philippines Los Baños on November 12 to join the protest on the arrival of US President Donald Trump.

The 15 minors were the last to be released from being held in Bahay Pag-asa in Muntinlupa City. There were a total of 20 minors among the participants of Lakbayan Southern Tagalog, who were arrested on November 15 during the police’s violent dispersal in barangay Sucat.

The five minors aged 15 below were already released on November 17 as they were found to have no criminal liability.

The more than 200 adults who were part of the Lakbayan were earlier released on the night of November 18.

This contradicted the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) claim on November 18, that all 236 delegates of Southern Tagalog were released. The 15 minors were only released in the afternoon of November 19.

“Despite days of delaying tactics and bureaucratic processes that kept the minors detained for four days after illegal arrest and parents waiting in distress – returning everyday and waiting outside overnight – with the pressure of child rights advocates, lawyers, and church organizations, the children are now free,” Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns said.

“As we celebrate this collective victory, we also continue to demand for the immediate release of the nine illegally arrested and detained protesters at the Liwasang Bonifacio last November 15. One of them is a minor and currently remains at the Manila Youth Reception Center (MYRC),” the group said in their social media page.

According to Salinlahi, the children were denied their rights to counsel as the Bahay Pag-asa Head blocked the lawyers and paralegals from talking to them.

Salinlahi stressed that these children suffered police brutality and their longer detention only makes their violations of their rights extend much further.

“Bahay Pag-asa is mandated to protect and rehabilitate children—not become an instrument for prolonging their detention and suppressing their rights,” Salinlahi said in a statement.

For the National Union of People’s Lawyer (NUPL) the Philippine National Police (PNP) must be held accountable for their brutality against activists who are only exercising their right to protest. “These findings expose the fundamental weakness of the PNP’s case. Having arrested and charged hundreds of individuals in one sweeping operation, the police could not even sufficiently distinguish the alleged acts of one respondent from another.”

Meanwhile, three students of the University of Makati (UMak) were also released on November 19.

The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office dismissed the cases that were filed against the students. These are alarm and scandal under Article 155 of the Revised Penal Code and resistance and disobedience to an agent of a person in authority under Article 151 of the same code.

The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office said in its resolution, “The evidence on record shows that the actions of (three students), were made specifically to voice out certain political and social grievances and not the purpose of causing general disturbance or public disorder.”

Lawyer Jose Topacio of the Alliance of Nationalist and Genuine Labor Organizations-Kilusang Mayo Uno (ANGLO-KMU) meanwhile pointed out that the three students were released only after six days of continuous confinement at the Taguig City Police Station, way past the time periods prescribed by Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code.

“We are also alarmed at the brazen displays of intimidation by the police, where the detainees were repeatedly told that the police intended to hold them for six days, that detailed files about them were being compiled since the Grand Hyatt protest on 10 September, and that their arrest should serve as a ‘lesson’ to them,” Topacio told Bulatlat in a message.

Topacio also noted how Taguig City police shouted at the visiting relatives of the students and repeatedly asked to move away from the station to other parts of the Taguig City Hall complex while conferring with counsel.

“Nevertheless, we are grateful for their release and would like to thank their counsels during the inquest, Attys. Krizza Hedriana and Ana Perez from the University of Makati for rendering timely aid in the morning,” said Topacio who was part of the quick reaction team on November 13.

Progressive groups continue to call for the release of the remaining nine individuals under the custody of the Manila Police District (including one minor remaining in MYRC).

According to the Alliance of Concerned Teachers-Philippines, their inquest proceedings concluded on November 16.

“Three days have passed, yet there is still no resolution. The prosecutor is currently delaying the signing of their resolution. This harassment has no legal basis, and they must be released immediately. The abusive police officers must be held accountable for their violence against ordinary citizens,” the group said. One of their volunteers was among those who were arrested.

Progressive groups said that what happened on November 15 was the biggest mass arrest in a single day under the Marcos Jr. administration. (with reports from Anne Marxze D. Umil) (DAA)

title: 3 UN experts alarmed over mass detention during ASEAN Summit
content:
Three United Nations Special Rapporteurs have publicly called out the Philippine government over the reported detention of more than 300 people during protests at the opening of the ASEAN 2026 summit, warning that the arrests point to a broader squeeze on dissent.

The mass arrest happened last November 15, 2026 when demonstrations broke out across Metro Manila to coincide with the regional summit to oppose the U.S.-led Pax technology and mining initiative and the presence of U.S. President Donald Trump. They were released on the night of November 18, following a decision of the Muntinlupa prosecutor.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

Among the arrested are mostly members of the Southern Tagalog group Lakbayan in Muntinlupa City, alongside media workers including student journalists, and progressive groups at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, and Bulacan.

Andrea Bolaños Vargas, Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights defenders, said she is concerned by reports of police violence against peaceful protesters and is monitoring the safety and protection of human rights defenders.

“I have received worrying information about the situation and am closely monitoring developments, including regarding the safety and protection of human rights defenders,” Vargas said.

Gina Romero, UN Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, wrote she received reports that security officials earlier in the week urged groups to hold off on protests until after the summit, reportedly to avoid a bad image before foreign visitors.

#Philipines today's police behaviour mirror a wider crackdown on dissent in the country. I have been receiving worrisome information about sedition subpoenas for anti-corruption protests, authorities tagging student leaders as "wanted", military home visits & campus lockdowns 3/

“Peaceful protests are not a PR question, they are a (human rights) issue,”

Romero added that this goes beyond the image of the ASEAN Summit taking place in the country. “(The) Philippines prior protests on related issues such as the pax silica have also been harassed,” she wrote.

Astrid Riano, Special Rapporteur on the right to a clean, safe and healthy environment, also said she is closely following the situation in Manila and in demonstrations elsewhere in the country.

Read: ‘Make Pax Silica deal public’

Riano also emphasized that ASEAN’s efforts should be aligned on its declaration to the right of a safe, clean, healthy, and sustainable environment at the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur on October 26, 2025. This declaration aimed to address climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental pollution.

“The right to a #healthyenvironment includes access to information and public participation, which includes peaceful demonstrations,” Riano said.

The same police brutality during Anti-Pax Silica protests are also prevalent across the regions of the country.

In Cebu City, rights group Karapatan Central Visayas has recorded reports of at least 10 attempted arrests and about 20 people injured in the police dispersal, with one protester reportedly rushed to the emergency room.

On November 18, 2026, the arrested protesters were released after three days in detention. Global civil society alliance CIVICUS is urging the Philippine government to investigate police restrictions and excessive force against protesters during the ASEAN Summit in Manila. (RVO)

People in Mindanao added their voices in opposing the United States (US)-led Pax Silica, an initiative that aims to establish an industrial hub that could displace Indigenous and peasant communities.

Like in many areas, mobilizations led by various organizations in the island became massive when Filipinos were waiting for the arrival of US President Donald Trump for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

In Mindanao State University – Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT), an estimated 3,000 students have reportedly joined the walkout protest on November 17 to observe the National Students’ Day, highlighting their calls to reject the Pax Silica initiative and its proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park project to be constructed in New Clark City, Tarlac.

The said 1,600-hectare industrial hub is being promoted as an economic security zone (ESZ) that would strengthen shared supply chains in semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies.

title: No red carpet for empire: State repression and the fight against Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them.

6,000-strong at Liwasang Bonifacio alone—and the numbers continue to surge as protesters march toward the PICC as U.S. President Donald Trump sets foot on Philippine soil. For over a century, U.S. imperialism has plundered this territory and oppressed its people, dating back to how it usurped the Katipunan’s hard-won 1896 triumph over Spanish colonialism. This is not the first time the Filipino people have fiercely rejected a Trump visit; they rose in protest during the ASEAN Summit in November 2017, and they are rising again.

The Filipino public’s refusal to welcome Trump—standing in sharp contrast to the Marcos Jr. administration’s eagerness to accommodate Washington—cannot justify the sweeping crackdown on activists exercising their fundamental rights to assembly, expression, and association. International observers have been alarmed by the scale and intensity of police brutality under Marcos Jr., which echoes the state terror unleashed over half a century ago under the U.S.-backed Martial Law dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.—a regime only toppled in 1986 after a protracted, heroic struggle against U.S. imperialism and its client-dictator.

Yet this violence is not merely a nostalgic return to his father’s Martial Law era; it is the continuation of an unbroken war against the poor. In the Philippine countryside, landless peasants live in a state of perpetual siege, battered by recurring tiempo muerto (dead seasons), massacres, and state-backed counterinsurgency campaigns that target cooperative leaders and their families. In the cities, whenever public anger boils over—such as during last year’s mass anti-corruption demonstrations—state repression falls hardest on patriotic youth—students and urban poor—the very demographics with the greatest stake in systemic change.

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them. Before a single bomb is dropped, it secures the physical pillars of modern warfare and artificial intelligence—water, energy grids, land, and semiconductor supply chains—within allied borders. Designated as the United States’ key strategic ally in Asia, the Philippines is being positioned as a primary resource frontline.

The lethal purpose of Pax Silica’s weaponry and intelligence apparatus is already on full display in Palestine—one of its primary targets, and the sharpest expression of a settler colonialism that never stops settling. As this colonial project expands, so too does the global infrastructure required to endlessly reproduce the war machine. That relentless reproduction of war stands in stark, irreconcilable opposition to the social reproduction of human life and labor. This is precisely why the Filipino working poor and youth are determined to junk Pax Silica and reject the presence of a war criminal like Trump. For us Filipinos, defiance against this weaponized interdependence is an imperative of national self-defense.

In oppressed nations like the Philippines, where the people are actively working to resolve their primary contradiction against U.S. imperialism, defending the social reproduction of life and labor inevitably requires taking to the streets. When protesters march despite knowing they will face state violence and police brutality, it is not because they invite harm or court repression; rather, it is how the peoples of oppressed nations shed the illusions of safety and docility under U.S. imperialist diktat. Only by confronting that violence do we reclaim our dignity—a dignity rooted in land, national patrimony, solidarity, and the camaraderie in struggle that Filipinos have always been proud of and known for.

This collective resolve has deep historical roots. From the basic masses and Indigenous Peoples to professionals, students, cultural workers, and progressive lawmakers, nationwide opposition remains firm. That same power found historic, legal expression on September 12, 1991, when the Philippine Senate voted to reject the renewal of the U.S. basing treaty—a victory won through a relentless mass campaign against the occupation of ancestral lands, the plunder of our resources, the systemic abuse of Filipino women and children, and the stripping of our national sovereignty.

Recent global events underscore the urgency of this struggle. The year opened with a devastating U.S. assault on Venezuela that claimed over a hundred lives and saw the abduction and unlawful detention of President Nicolás Maduro and First Combatant Cilia Flores. Weeks later, U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran killed over 150 schoolchildren in Minab along with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. While the world was initially stunned, grief has hardened into sustained anti-imperialist resistance across West Asia. Simultaneously, mass protests in cities like Paris reveal that even in the imperial core, capitalism’s “peacetime” delivers only austerity, state abuse, and economic precarity.

An imperialist world order offers no viable future for humanity or the biosphere. Persisting down the path championed by leaders like Trump and Marcos Jr. stands in direct opposition to historical progress, ecological survival, and the basic material conditions needed for human life to thrive. Time and again, we show—and are reminded—that our identity as a free and dignified people can only be forged through class struggle against U.S. imperialism. Today’s mobilization is nothing short of historic: it transforms the memory of an anti-colonial revolution usurped by foreign powers into the undeniable thunder of resolute footsteps, marching forward and defending the nation.

title: ‘No red carpet’ for Trump’s arrival in the Philippines
content:

title: Romulos Robiños
content:
Romulos “Mulong” Robiños, a 24-year-old tricycle driver was abducted from his home in Angeles city, Pampanga on November 17, 2006 by suspected state forces. The armed suspects barged into their house at 12:30 midnight looking for his sister Leny Robiños, an activist. When they did not find her, they instead forcibly took Mulong. They threatened his mother Lolita that she will not see Mulong again unless she makes Leni “surrender”.

In 2007, the Supreme Court issued a writ of amparo and ordered military camps to allow the search for Mulong. However, the search failed to find Mulong or any other victim of enforced disappearance. He remains missing 20 years later.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Overcoming police brutality, protests continue vs. Trump, Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates held an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

“Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

No amount of police brutality could hold back the progressive groups from continuing their protest today, November 16. They gathered at the Liwasang Bonifacio and strongly condemned the Marcos Jr. administration for its subservience to foreign interests.

“We feel more courage now that there are many people who chose to stand alongside our fight for our ancestral lands,” Ayta elder Nelson De Guzman told Bulatlat in Filipino. “Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

De Guzman is among the delegation of the Ayta-Hungey community from Capas, Tarlac who went to Manila to join the series of protests against the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump and the reported signing of the Pax Silica framework agreement.

He said, “They are lying when they said that indigenous peoples will not be affected [by Pax Silica]. We are here to prove them wrong and stand for what is right.”

The first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit on November 15 began with a series of arbitrary mass arrests of close to 300 activists, students, journalists, and community leaders.

Hundreds of the arrested individuals were part of the Lakbayan Southern Tagalog who were supposed to hold a campout in Liwasang Bonifacio to attend the series of protests in Manila.

They have been detained for more than 24 hours at Camp Bagong Diwa in Bicutan.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code limits detention without charges to 12 [light penalties], 18,[correctional penalties] or 36 hours [capital penalties]. It also guarantees the accused’s right to legal counsel at any time.

Lawyers, paralegals, and human rights investigators were only allowed entry to Camp Bagong Diwa after six hours of negotiation with the police.

“From the first day since we started our lakbayan (collective march), the repression never stopped. They tried to sabotage our program, the wheels of our vehicles, up to the massive deployment of police officers within our camp-out area,” human rights defender Paul Tagle, who is part of the Southern Tagalog delegation, said in Filipino in a press conference.

He said that detained individuals are being threatened with charges under the Public Assembly Act (Batas Pambansa Blg. 880), a remnant of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.’s dictatorship, which he described as a complete “madness” since it is the police who exercised violent intervention.

Read: Bayan hits ‘Marcosian’ tactics against protesters

At least 500 policemen are reportedly stationed in the entry and exit points in University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, where some 200 Ayta and their supporters held a campout.

Cristina Palabay, secretary general of human rights group Karapatan, demanded accountability from police officers and commanders who ordered the violent interference. She emphasized that the denial coming from state security forces, particularly the National Police Commission (Napolcom), rings hollow as the police brutality was properly documented by the journalists and activists, publicized in the social media.

“The fact is,” said Palabay, “the PNP has long been besmirching the uniform. Yesterday’s incidents of police brutality have not been the first, nor will they be the last, given the vociferous statements issued by the PNP’s talking heads, and their consistent denials of the truth.”

Moreover, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) said that neither the ASEAN Summit nor Trump’s visit guarantees the suspension of peoples’ right to protest and peaceful assembly.

“The Constitution guarantees the people’s right to protest. Peaceful assembly is no crime, while the law requires maximum tolerance and protects participants in otherwise peaceful assemblies from criminal liability,” the NUPL said in a statement.

The group also demanded release of the detained individuals, the police to pull back from UP’s gates to allow the protest delegation to reach the assembly sites unharmed, and the accountability of state security personnel responsible for unlawful arrests and assaults.

The Philippine National Police deployed more than 23,000 personnel coming from the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protection, and other concerned agencies.

Igorot youth leader Funa-ay Claver, secretary general of indigenous group Katribu, said that they have long prepared for the protest actions.

“The repression of the administration is in full force, all to stop our Indigenous Peoples from asserting their rights and aspirations. But we see that most of us reached here in Manila to fight together despite the long, tedious journey,” said Claver.

Another youth leader, Lance Alba of Anakbayan, said during the protest today: “The violence, repression, and arrests never stopped. But so are we. Our camp-out remains. And we are ready to continue this until November 18.”

“Protest marches that attempt to go beyond designated spaces or barricades, are still protected by the right to peaceful assembly, and must not be forcibly or violently dispersed,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, Section Director of Amnesty International Philippines.

Article 5 of the United Nations Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials states that it is prohibited to inflict, instigate, or tolerate any act of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, nor they can invoke superior orders or exceptional circumstances as a justification.

“The PNP must take steps to practice restraint and strict adherence to international standards on the use of force. Any use of force must be a measure of last resort, and should be in line with the principles of necessity and proportionality,” said Santos.

Meanwhile, for Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) “now is the best time to speak out and hold Marcos accountable for his treasonous sell-out of the country’s resources when the country is under international spotlight.”

The group said the world needs to know that farmers and Indigenous Peoples are being evicted from their lands because of the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

“While Marcos is rolling out a red carpet welcome for war criminal Donald Trump, the Filipino people are opposing his state visit. After his party’s embarrassing defeat in the midterm polls, Trump is being greeted by a gigantic ‘protest wave’ in the Philippines,” Bayan said.

“People’s protests are not organized for the convenience of those in power. We protest to inconvenience those who abuse their power like the fascist puppet Marcos Jr. regime,” they added. (AMU, RVO)

title: ‘Unconstitutional’ — lawyers on checkpoints blocking, delaying protesters
content:
Southern Tagalog delegates negotiating with the police who block their way going to Liwasang Bonifacio. Photo from UPLB Perspective

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost.”

As police continue to block protesters from different places using checkpoints, progressive lawyers said the police are interrupting not only the rights of the people to protest but also of Filipinos who are working during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Delegates from Southern Tagalog who held the Lakbayan ng Timog Katalugan (Southern Tagalog caravan) starting on November 12, faced police brutality during their march to Liwasang Bonifacio.

Previously, they have been repeatedly blocked by police forces. Reports from UPLB Perspective shows punctured tires from the vehicles used by the delegates. The harassment continued where police disrupted the delegates when they barricaded the road at midnight to prevent them from moving forward.

On November 15, police brutality took over as they violently arrested almost 270 delegates while holding a peaceful mobilization. As of this writing, the National Union of People’s Lawyers and Koalisyong Makabayan have gained access to those arrested.

In the University of the Philippines, hundreds of police were deployed to man checkpoints at the exit points. The PICC and nearby areas were also heavily guarded. Aside from these checkpoints, there are also other checkpoints conducted in the borders of several provinces and the National Capital Region.

In an interview, National Union of Peoples’ Lawyer (NUPL) Ephraim “Rey” Cortez underscores that mass deployment of checkpoints within the area violates freedom of expression and right to peaceful assembly that is protected under the Philippine constitution.

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost,” Cortez asserted.

Cortez also explained that freedom of expression should include the right of people to protest not just in any designated freedom park such as the Liwasang Bonifacio but anywhere without needing to secure a permit.

In Batas Pambansa Bldg. 880, going to freedom park to protest does not need a permit or any travel pass. Lawyers like the NUPL argue that blocking protesters while officials cannot identify clear and present danger is unconstitutional.

The said law has been facing criticism by NUPL stating that “this dictatorship-era law that places constitutional rights of the people to collective action under a system of prior state approval.”

Aside from rally permit arguments, Cortez added that traffic regulations should not also be used as a tool to suppress or stop the people going to freedom park where they can protest to amplify their call against police brutality and opposition to Pax Silica where thousands of Ayta and local farmers will lose their livelihood.

“As long as there is no clear and present danger, [it] cannot prevail over the exercise of constitutional guaranteed rights,” Cortez explained.

As there are no specific laws on checkpoints, the Supreme Court has previous decisions such as the Valmonte vs. De Villa, which states that checkpoint is not illegal but law enforcement shall be limited to visual search.

In Aniag Jr. vs COMELEC, it is stated that police should only have access to a vehicle if they have probable cause or voluntary consent. None of the ruling states that checkpoints can be used to block protesters, especially going to freedom park.

“You are conducting a checkpoint because there is an impending criminal act to be committed. But if the checkpoint is used because of protest, it violates their constitutional rights […] You can’t put the blame on protesters as they are continuously moving and exercising their rights,” Cortez said.

According to Cortez, it is not the people who participated in the rally causing traffic, the blame should fall on the police who continuously block the protesters’ way to raise their legitimate concerns.

As police brutality continues, progressive groups vow to push through with their protests to amplify the call of the marginalized groups especially to Indigenous and local communities who will be affected once the Pax Silica is officially constructed. (AMU, RVO)

title: Groups condemn police brutality, state repression against anti-Pax Silica protesters
content:
Police officers arrest a protester during a protest in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 15, 2026. Photo by Adrian Puse/Altermidya

MANILA — “Trump was given a red carpet but the Filipino people are given fascism and repression, and are prevented from expressing their opposition to Pax Silica.”

This is the statement of Dr. Ganni Tapang, leaf convener of the Network Opposed to Pax Silica.

Representatives of different progressive groups condemned the state’s attacks against Filipino activists, journalists, and Indigenous people in a press conference at Vinzon’s compound at the University of the Philippines–Diliman.

Around 500 personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) were spotted surrounding the perimeter of campus. They were stationed around the entrance and exits of campus, along Katipunan Avenue, University Avenue, and College of Science among others.

Tapang, also the former Dean of the College of Science, condemned the collusion of the Philippine government with the US, specifically Marcos Jr.’s enabling the Pax Silica Initiative to plunder the country.

“The PNP should be defending our rights and not curtailing them, and following the orders of Donald Trump and President Marcos,” Tapang said.

The Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica launched on campus on Friday, November 13, and will continue until November 16. This was participated by 200 Ayta, including 50 from Cordillera, 500 farmers and youth from Central Luzon, and many volunteers and community members.

Although UP is a sanctuary campus, student journalists from the College of Mass Communication covering the protests suffered from attempted arrests.

Dr. Ma. Diosa Labiste, dean of the UP College of Media and Communications, said that this is the police’s attempt to prevent legitimate dissent in the course of the ASEAN summit.

“We demand the police to recognize the citizens to participate in protest actions,” said Labiste. “We will hold the police accountable if our students are harmed when they are doing their job as campus journalists.”

“Journalism is not illegal,” said Yvo Asis, multimedia editor of the Philippine Collegian. He shared about a student journalist from UP who was arrested in Sucat, Muntinlupa while on the ground.

The police did not read to them the Miranda rights and later on brought a truck full of people to Camp Bagong Diwa. Over 300 were arrested, with the largest contingent coming from Southern Tagalog.

“It is the democratic right of the Filipino masses to spread the developments of Pax Silica.” Paul Viuya, Chairperson of BAYAN Central Luzon, said that these arrests expose the true face of fascism in our country.

Of those arrested, twelve were injured, including someone who fainted and was still kicked in the head by the police, according to Teacher Kat Ortega, president of the All UP Academic Employees Union.

Ortega also condemned the arrest of three students of the University of Makati while participating in the November 13 nationwide student walkout. “They are not criminals. They are just peacefully expressing their indignation,” she said.

Activists in Liwasang Bonifacio shared to Ortega how the police scattered human feces and urine around Freedom Park on November 15. They also took the rallyists’ belongings, and slashed the tires of the activists’ trucks while they were setting up for the protest.

The Philippine government allotted P22.9 billion (US$358 million) for hosting the ASEAN Summit.. Ortega said that these could have been used for social services and building classrooms that serve the Filipino people. Instead, it is used for the advancement of Pax Silica, which will take the country’s water, electricity, and labor power.

“We call on the PNP. Arrest Atong Ang, Zaldy Co, Bato dela Rosa, and all of the corrupt politicians. Block Donald Trump, who wages war against the people of the world,” said Ortega. “They are the true criminals who destroy peoples’ lives.”

Amid repression, Erich Jones Escototo, convener of UP Against Pax Silica (UPAX) said that nothing could silence the voices of the oppressed Filipino masses.

“The Filipino people continue to resist.” Escototo called on fellow students to join the protests in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 17 where different sectors from all over the country will express their indignation.

“What the masses want is the freedom to protest,” said Tapang, calling on the Filipino people to stand for their right to protest and to convey their demands and opposition. (RVO)

title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

Read: Groups decry surveillance of KMU office in Southern Mindanao

Marklen called for an end to any form of harassment and intimidation against families of the disappeared, pointing out that achieving justice is their only goal. (RVO)

title: Artists, Ayta sing vs Pax Silica
content:
Photo by Shannia Angel Cabuello

Artists and other advocates amplified their opposition against a US-led initiative through song.

On November 6, an artist group launched the anti-Pax Silica anthem “Get Off Our Lands” in a solidarity night filled with protest songs.

Produced by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP), the song was accompanied by a documentary music video featuring the Ayta community in Sitio Kalangitan, whose ancestral lands and natural resources are threatened by displacement and plunder.

Through the song, CAP aimed to expose the false promises behind the Pax Silica and to condemn those in power who allowed it.

Cultural performances and solidarity messages completed the program as part of the Trump Out campaign and the ‘12 Days of Protests’, building up the major protest actions on November 16 and 17.

Ayta elders also attended the solidarity night and expressed their strong rejection of Pax Silica, chanting “Ako Labay Ya Pax Silica!” (I don’t like Pax Silica!).

They led a community dance ritual to drive away “bad spirits,” which they associate with the Pax Silica Initiative and the impending visit of US President Donald Trump for the ASEAN Summit.

Ayta Chieftain Nelson De Guzman countered the statement of Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang that no Indigenous community would be affected by the Pax Silica Initiative. He said that no proper consultation was conducted within their community.

“They learned that they were being driven away from their land even before they knew about the project,” said Sandiwa Network project coordinator Gina Cambronero.

“The Pax Silica will kill our future. We nurtured our lands. We cannot allow foreigners to claim it,” said Ayta Indigenous woman Tessie Sanchez.

Sanchez told Bulatlat that planting rice, taro, and sweet potato helped support her seven children. She feared that the signing of the agreement could dry their water sources and take away their farmlands.

“The ruling class used the term pax which meant peace. But is there peace in it? They use it as instruments for deception,” Cambronero said.

“We just want peace in our tribe and in our land,” De Guzman said in the song’s documentary music video.

Around 20,000 peasants and 15,000 Ayta could be reportedly displaced once its Artificial Intelligence hub was established on the 1,620 hectares of land in Tarlac.

The anthem started by introducing the Philippines as a friendly Southeast Asian country that shares its homeland to everyone, even to foreign ones.

The music video explained that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. volunteered to give the agricultural and ancestral lands in Tarlac to the United States to establish an Economic Security Zone.

CAP said that the establishment of an Artificial Intelligence hub in Tarlac and the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) in Subic Bay, Clark, Manila and Batangas that claims of job creation and economic security are false promises. The group said that it only “prioritizes corporate profits and militarization, fueling war for the US benefit.”

“In the past years, we have always been at a disadvantage with US relations. There are already several trade agreements that only lead to our losses,” said Attorney Rey Cortez of National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL).

Cortez added in a solidarity message that it only allowed for the United States to mine the country’s lands and determine how to exploit its resources. He described the government’s marketing of the country’s environment and sovereignty as unconstitutional, as only the Filipinos are allowed to explore the Philippines’ critical minerals.

“Development should not be measured by the number of investments, infrastructure, and technology advancements. Its effect on the people, community, and environment must also be analysed,” said College of Social Work and Community Development Dean and CAP member Justin Nicolas.

Arthur Cadungon of CAP and writer of Get Off Our Lands said that the anthem is not just for the fight against the Pax Silica Initiative, but also a song of protest against the reclamation of Manila Bay, Laguna Lake, and Pasig River Expressway (PAREX).

“An example of this is the Laguna Lake, which before sources at least 40% of protein food sources like mussels and freshwater fish tilapia,” said Environmental Advocates group Nilad coordinator Samantha Yzabel.

She added that fishing has become difficult for the communities near Laguna Lake as the destruction of ecosystems and pollution worsens. She also stressed that the Manila Bay and Pasig River are being destroyed, while communities continue to be displaced and deprived of livelihood.

Cadungon dedicated the song to the trees that were cut along the Quirino highway, and for the Filipinos who were drowned by flood and were neglected by the people in power.

“This is also a fight with the courageous people of the Kasibu community in Nueva Vizcaya, around the nation, and other countries that are being stripped bare by imperialists,” Cadungon said.

Artists and cultural workers strengthened their rejection of the Pax Silica that facilitates the use of Artificial Intelligence saying that it undermines human creativity.

“Trump’s visit means taking away my workforce. It means building of AI hubs that would replace years of artist’s struggle in honing their crafts,” handcrafter Aila Bathan said.

Just like the Ayta Indigenous Peoples and communities in Central Luzon, Bathan said that Pax Silica means death of their lives and livelihoods.

“True prosperity promotes people’s dignity, strengthens communities, nurtures the environment, and advocates for overall well-being,” said Dean Nicolas, calling on the Filipinos to be critical and stand firm for social justice.

CAP Secretary-General Edge Ungayuren emphasized that once farmers that cultivate the lands are threatened, even ordinary Filipinos are affected. “We believe that we must take a stand in this issue because it would kill our lands, bodies of water, farmers, and Indigenous Peoples. Our culture is rooted in our lands and bodies of water. If these will be gone, our culture will also be gone,”

CAP urged artists, cultural workers, and the public to use their art and the anti-Pax Silica anthem to take their resistance on the streets and get imperialists off the nation’s land. (AMU, DAA)

title: ‘Get Off Our Lands’ political pop vs  Pax SIlica
content:
Photo by Shannia Cabuello/Bulatlat

It was a hot night on November 6 and Z compound, a food park at Teachers’ Village, was already brimming with enthusiasts for the world premiere of the anti-Pax Silica song anthem “Get Off Our Lands” by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP).

Highlight of the night was the launch of the music video, enhanced by a separate lyric video, and the actual performance of CAP’s music pool.

The song starts in a slow tempo, then pulled off unsuspectingly into a high-energy sound by the rhythm of various instruments and the piercing wails of Bayang Barrios. Soaring vocals join in, combined with addictive hooks and riffs that sustain the track’s hype and momentum. The melody is sharp and catchy, flowing seamlessly into a songwriting that has easy recall yet nails it as a serious political critique.

Without a doubt, the song title sets the core message, but the punch is delivered by the chants “Tutulan, labanan, reject Pax Silica!” which can draw even a crowd into a sea of resounding voices and clenched fists.

“Get Off Our Lands” is indeed a battlecry, a sonic weapon, against the US-led Pax Silica. An initiative or agreement in collusion with the Marcos Jr regime, Pax Silica would plunder the country’s critical minerals for the US war machine. Its plan to set up Artificial Intelligence hubs would also deprive communities of scarce water resources and energy and poison the environment. Even artists are up in arms as they might lose not just their jobs but the authenticity of their art and craft as well.

In the video, the cries of the Aytas of Capas, Tarlac, probably the first victims of displacement, has sounded off the people’s indignation. It is an emotional, yet serene plea to stop, reject, or shot down Pax Silica, not just for themselves but also for all those who will be affected. That CAP made the Aytas, this peace-loving indigenous community, speak for themselves is a stark contrast to the destruction and violence that awaits them, and the nation in due time.

It is a grim scenario. But the night did not leave the viewers and listeners in quiet rage. Then CAP’s music pool commanded the stage. The explosion of energetic sound with astounding raw vocals brought bodies suddenly jumping on their feet, eager to sway and vibe, and without a prompt turned to the lyric video, singing, chanting, dancing. The crowd, mostly millennials and GenZs seemed to have lost it. To everyone’s applause one band member even quipped – “this is not AI”.

Political pop is not just about poverty and sufferings, domination and violence. As much as it is expository, it is also celebratory. That one night in November proved it. The awakening was palpable, though many of those who attended were probably already woke. The crowd knew the fears, the dangers, the darkness of Pax Silica. Still the spirits were high. Optimism seemed to fill the air seeing the people’s defiance on screen: whether in the Aytas’ soft words, the sincerity of the artists, the militance of mass leaders, the fiery protest actions layered on top of the music’s vibrancy. Much as Pax Silica brings doom, the people’s collective struggle depicted in the song or video brings hope and much more. And the crowd felt it and the response was electric.

In addition, the passion, the conviction, and the emotion that artists have poured into “Get Off Our Lands” was borne out of their own experiences. So it has become and remains organic. The artistas ng bayan spent days with the Aytas in their own community, immersed in their own life stories, felt their surroundings, and delved into their culture.

And so it was that the making of the song did not become a private treasure. The Aytas participated and contributed some lines. So did a roster of composers, songwriters, performers, recording engineers and fellow bands who supported, gave comments, reactions, put in a word or two, before the song ‘s debut. From a shared experience with the Aytas the song became a truly collective collaboration of artists who believed in the same goal.

Now all it takes is to spread and amplify the song in a manner so massive it awakens people to the dangers of Pax Silica and move them into action. CAP has summoned a clarion call to all interested parties to do covers, play the song in all types of events or performances, and saturate social media.

November is also the month that US President Donald Trump is coming to the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, and anticipation is high that the Pax Silica agreement will be signed. By then the No to Pax Silica movement shall be ready, Trump will feel the heat of being unwelcomed, and slammed by the music “Get Off Our Lands”.

title: Investigate police, doctors involved in Duterte’s ‘drug war’
content:
Forensic pathologist Dr. Raquel Fortun, also a member of the commission, presents one of the questionable certificates during the commission's truth-telling session last Friday. (Truth Commission photo)

The Truth Commission has called on the Philippine government to investigate the police officers’ misconduct and promotion and the doctors’ questionable death certificates in the course of the “drug war” campaign of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

“My son was alive when they arrested him, but they killed him. They could’ve let him live. They did not show mercy, they planted drugs and guns,” Marissa Lazaro, mother of extrajudicial killing victim Cristopher Lazaro, said in Tagalog during the commission’s truth-telling session.

The Truth Commission pointed to a failed system for investigating deaths, marked by careless police and forensic work, and little concern for victims’ families. Lazaro’s account also showed that the police officers were asking money from her, indicating a potential trail of corruption.

Cristopher, 20, and Alberto Paragas, 32, died in police operations on August 5, 2017 in Marilao, Bulacan. Police reported that the two resisted (nanlaban) after an alleged attempted holdup. Cristopher’s friends also died hours earlier in Bocaue, a separate town in Bulacan.

Lazaro added, “They asked me to sign a waiver, indicating that I consented to their illegal operation. I did not sign it. They told me: the day will come that I will seek their help. I told them, what help could you give my son? You killed him. He’s already dead.”

A similar incident happened to Marissa Quiamco, sister of Alberto, after she paid the P10,000 fee to release the cadaver of her brother. A police officer asked her and Alberto’s partner to sign a document, indicating consent for the operation but they refused to sign.

“I wish I could fight for my brother. Even my neighbors asked me to file a complaint. But I told them: we don’t have money. We don’t have the capacity or resources to get a lawyer,” Quiamco said during the truth-telling session. “I’m only earning enough to help my mother and father.”

In October, an analysis of public records by the Truth Commission recorded a pattern that commanding police officers were promoted and reassigned, instead of being subjected to criminal and administrative sanctions.

Lito Patay, who commanded Batasan police station that killed 108 people in drug operations during his term, was named chief of the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) in Central Luzon.

In Caloocan, the commission’s own records documented 284 killings in 2016, before the leadership of Chito Bersaluno in the City Police. During his watch, 105 more deaths were recorded from February to August 2017. He was removed from his post after the killing of Kian delos Santos. However, he was made police director of Bulacan Province in 2018 and promoted to the rank of brigadier general in 2022.

In 2020, human rights organizations flagged the reassignment of Debold Sinas, former chief of the Central Visayas Police Regional Office, to the National Capital Region. The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Regional Office said back then that Sinas’ watch in Central Visayas was marred by unresolved killings linked to the illegal drugs trade and the anti-insurgency campaign “Oplan Sauron.” Duterte appointed him as the Philippine National Police Chief on November 9, 2020, serving a six-month term. A year after, he was appointed as an undersecretary of the Office of the President.

Read: [LIST] Gross human rights violations under Debold Sinas

“Any inquiry must look at promotions as closely as it looks at cash payments,” said Christopher Magno, the commission’s executive director and an expert on state violence in the Philippines. “No police officer should gain in any way from the blood of people killed outside the law.”

Former Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) General Manager Royina Garma, who also served as Cebu City police chief under the Duterte administration, revealed the incentivization of police officers through the “Davao Model” in a quad committee hearing of the House of Representatives in 2024.

“First is the reward if the suspect is killed. Second is the funding of planned operations. Third is the refund of operational expenses,” Garma said, stressing that the rewards started from P20,000 ($343.95) to P1 million ($17,197.50), depending on the profile of the suspects. She said that the rewards were only meant for killings, not for the arrest of the drug suspects.

During the quad committee hearing, it was also revealed that rewards for anti-drug operations by the police involved several key figures, including then-Special Assistant to the President Bong Go, an individual known as “Muking” from the Presidential Management Staff, a “Pedro” from the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, and former National Police Commission (Napolcom) Commissioner Edilberto Leonardo, who handled the distribution of the payments.

Read: Duterte’s testimony affirmed that drug-related extrajudicial killings a state policy — right groups

Questionable death certification

The Truth Commission also called on the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) to investigate the medical doctors behind the questionable death certificates of extrajudicial killing victims.

A letter submitted by the Truth Commission on November 9 reads: “Accurate death certification is essential to establishing the truth about the circumstances of a person’s death. Where death certificates contain inaccurate, incomplete, or potentially misleading information, families may be deprived of an accurate official record of what happened to their loved ones.”

In the 150 extrajudicial killing victims examined by forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun, who is also a commissioner of the Truth Commission, at least 13 death certificates listed causes of death that did not match her findings. Among these were the cases of Alberto and Cristopher.

Fortun’s findings on Alberto’s forensic examination indicated that the manner of death was homicide. His death certificate stated no clear reason and labeled “for autopsy.” Fortun’s team tried to ask for an autopsy report but to no avail.

Christopher’s death certificate and medico-legal report issued by the Philippine National Police also did not match. The former document indicates that the cause of death was a “gunshot wound (to the trunk) and left lower extremity”, while the medico-legal stated “gunshot wound (of the) head and left lower extremity.”

She also questioned whether the doctor who documented ligature marks on Christopher’s wrists had been free to challenge the police. “This is very glaring. The pictures of the crime scene were also very limited and messy. The documentation of the scene is so wrong.”

The letter requested the PRC, through the Board of Medicine, not only to investigate the doctors and the death certification process, but also to determine professional accountability, help protect and preserve the evidence of “drug war”, and examine whether similar practices occurred in other cases.

They also asked the PRC to work with the Philippine Statistics Authority, local civil registrars, and relevant health authorities in correcting the death certificates. The Philippine Medical Association (PMA)’s Ethics Committee will also be helpful in examining possible violations of the professional ethics.

“We emphasize that the purpose of this request is not to prejudge the responsibility of any physician, but to ensure that questionable death certifications are properly investigated, that relevant evidence is protected, and that accountability is pursued where warranted and in accordance with due process,” the letter added.

“They already killed our loved ones, now, they’re vilifying them. I will persevere in speaking up to let the public know the true circumstances of my son’s death. Not all victims of the war on drugs are drug addicts. And even if they’re addicts, it is not a justified reason to kill them,” Lazaro said. (RTS, DAA)

title: What’s at stake in Trump’s Manila visit?
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit to Manila for the ASEAN Summit happens in the wake of intensifying struggle between the U.S. and China for economic, technological, political, and military dominance in Asia. Washington aims to consolidate its strategic position in Southeast Asia, with the Philippines under Ferdinand Marcos Jr. playing an increasingly important role in advancing U.S. imperialist interests.

Trump arrives politically battered. The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, which handed both houses of Congress to the Democrats, represents a powerful repudiation of his administration’s policies. Trump’s unpopular U.S. war against Iran and his aggressive tariff policies and their disastrous economic consequences, such as rising living costs, contributed to widespread dissatisfaction among American voters.

The defeat further exposes the political crisis confronting U.S. imperialism. It reflects growing domestic opposition to policies that impose enormous economic and social costs on the American people while sustaining Washington’s aggressive military interventions and global ambitions.

But Trump’s weakened domestic position does not mean that the White House will abandon its imperialist agenda abroad. On the contrary, the administration may seek to demonstrate U.S. power through new military, economic, and diplomatic agreements. Trump could use his visit to Manila to project strength and secure strategic commitments to counter the political setback at home.

The central objective of Washington’s ASEAN agenda is to preserve U.S. supremacy in the face of China’s expanding economic and military power. Southeast Asia occupies a crucial place in this rivalry. It sits astride strategic maritime routes and contains vital manufacturing centers, mineral resources, emerging digital markets, and production networks essential to the world economy.

For U.S. imperialism, maintaining influence over ASEAN means safeguarding its military reach while securing access to markets, technology infrastructure, critical minerals, and industrial supply chains. The U.S. seeks to organize these strategic assets around its own economic and national-security priorities, particularly by reducing dependence on Chinese-controlled production networks.

At the same time, China is expanding its own economic and strategic influence through trade, investment, infrastructure, and military power. This competition between rival great powers seeks to expand their influence over the region’s resources, markets, territory, and political decisions.

Washington’s military agenda was made explicit during the ASEAN defense ministers’ meetings in Cebu in October, when Pete Hegseth, Trump’s so-called Secretary of War, proposed a new framework for U.S.–ASEAN defense cooperation.

Under the language of maritime security and interoperability, Washington seeks to deepen military coordination, intelligence sharing, joint exercises, and naval cooperation with Southeast Asian governments. The proposal complements the expanding network of U.S. military alliances and access arrangements across the Indo-Pacific. It aims to strengthen its First Island Chain strategy to encircle and contain China. On the sidelines of the Cebu meeting, U.S. and Japanese defense officials discussed implementing a more effective denial-defense posture along this chain.

With its geographical location, the Philippines has become a crucial platform for this strategy. Under Marcos Jr., U.S. military access under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) has expanded from five to nine designated Philippine facilities. Washington and Manila are also increasing joint military exercises and deployments of advanced missile and unmanned systems. These arrangements strengthen the capacity of U.S. forces to operate in the South China Sea and potentially respond to a Taiwan Strait conflict.

So far, only two ASEAN countries have formal defense treaties with the U.S., namely the Philippines and Thailand. But all the other members, except for Myanmar, have various forms of extensive defense or military cooperation arrangements with the U.S. However, unlike its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) and related pacts with the Philippines, not all agreements with other ASEAN countries grant U.S. troops access to military installations, allow combat deployments, or entail an obligation to support U.S. military operations.

Hegseth’s proposal aims to move beyond separate military arrangements with individual ASEAN countries toward a more coordinated, ASEAN-wide structure for defense cooperation. Such a framework could strengthen the U.S. military’s regional presence and operational coordination without necessarily creating a formal military alliance. It will build on existing regional initiatives such as the ASEAN-U.S. Maritime Exercise (AUMX), the Southeast Asia Cooperation and Training (SEACAT), and other military exercises between ASEAN and the U.S. and American allies in the Indo-Pacific like Japan, Australia, and South Korea, focusing on naval coordination, maritime security and surveillance, and military interoperability.

Unlike the U.S., China lacks formal military treaties with any ASEAN member. However, it maintains defense cooperation memoranda of understanding with all of them except Myanmar, with which it nevertheless sustains substantial military equipment supplies, training, and defense ties. It also participates in the ASEAN-China Maritime Exercise (ACMX) as a regional initiative and maintains several bilateral and multilateral exercises with ASEAN members.

In terms of forward bases and military presence, the U.S. has several naval and air facilities in Thailand (U-Tapao airfield and Sattahip Naval Base) and Singapore (Changi Naval Base, Sembawang facilities and Paya Lebar Air Base), in addition to the nine EDCA sites in the Philippines, that allow the deployment of troops, prepositioning of supplies, and logistical support. China counters this with military infrastructure recently built in mainland Southeast Asia, specifically the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia and the Ban Keun aviation facility in Laos. Aside from the EDCA sites, the U.S. is also reinforcing its presence in the Philippines by deploying advanced weapons systems in strategic areas facing Taiwan and the South China Sea, while building defense-industrial infrastructure to support its military logistics and mobility through the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC). In response, China has fortified its position in the disputed maritime features of the South China Sea, establishing a military presence in the Spratly Islands with long airstrips, hangars, naval support facilities, and reportedly even air-defense and anti-ship missile systems.

The increasing militarization of Southeast Asia amid intensifying U.S.-China competition is exposing the people of the region to massive death and destruction. Such danger is aggravated by the political crisis the Trump regime faces following the midterm elections. It could further escalate regional tensions as Trump becomes more desperate and aggressive in projecting U.S. power abroad and asserting its control over territories it deems part of its spheres of influence to consolidate domestic support. To be sure, U.S. long-term strategic objectives in the Indo-Pacific have continued across successive Republican and Democratic regimes, but Trump’s post-midterm political calculations could further accelerate the region’s militarization and escalate tensions.

Battleground for strategic industries and supply chains

Another achievement Trump would likely seek during his Manila visit is finalizing an agreement with the Philippines to build an advanced manufacturing park within the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC). The 1,620-hectare Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park is a vital project for the Trump regime, as its success bolsters the feasibility of its Pax Silica initiative to counter China’s control over chokepoints of artificial intelligence (A.I.) supply chains, which have become a key arena of inter-imperialist competition for economic and military supremacy. Pax Silica is part of the broader U.S. strategic agenda to contain China and its rapid expansion.

Launched in December 2025, Pax Silica seeks to establish secure supply chains involving critical minerals, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure, and A.I. technologies among the U.S. and its trusted allies. It aims to strengthen American influence over the technologies and industrial inputs increasingly regarded as essential to economic and military power. Southeast Asia plays an important role in this strategy because of its substantial mineral resources, established electronics manufacturing industries, growing digital markets, and its location along crucial international trade routes.

A major challenge for the U.S. is how to break China’s grip on the region’s critical mineral resources, the most important raw materials to build A.I. and its infrastructure. China has overwhelming dominance in Southeast Asia’s mining investments, mineral processing, exports, and purchases. Indonesia, for instance, holds the world’s largest nickel reserves, accounting for 44% of the total, and China accounts for around 75% of Indonesia’s nickel refining capacity. The Philippines ranks sixth, and almost 72% of its nickel ore and concentrate exports go to China, while 28% go to Indonesia, with the former likely processed by Chinese refineries. Dismantling such monopoly control makes Pax Silica’s success in the Philippines high on Trump’s agenda for his visit to Manila.

China, meanwhile, is pursuing its own strategy to consolidate and expand its influence over the international A.I. supply chains and digital economy. A significant development was the establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) in July 2026, which presents itself as an inclusive intergovernmental institution that promotes cooperation, AI capacity building, and more equitable international governance.

Aside from the Philippines, Singapore is the only other ASEAN member among the 26 Pax Silica signatories. On the other hand, WAICO includes seven ASEAN countries among its 38 members: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, and Vietnam.

The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), scheduled to be signed at the Manila Summit, provides a potentially far-reaching framework through which the U.S.-China competition over A.I. supply chains could unfold.

Although negotiated by ASEAN member states, DEFA is being developed in an environment dominated by American and Chinese technology corporations. Its provisions on digital trade, cross-border data flows, electronic commerce, digital payments, and A.I. cooperation could profoundly influence who controls the region’s emerging digital economy. For the U.S., expanded ASEAN digital integration offers opportunities to consolidate its dominance in cloud computing, digital platforms, A.I. systems, financial technologies, and data infrastructure.

Resist imperialist domination and war in Southeast Asia

Trump’s upcoming Manila visit underscores how Southeast Asia is increasingly becoming a major theater for the competing economic, geopolitical, and military ambitions of the U.S. and China. Whether through military alliances and forward deployments, control over critical minerals and advanced technologies, or the reorganization of regional production networks, the two rival powers are seeking to secure their respective spheres of influence at the expense of the region’s sovereignty and the interests of its peoples.

For the Philippines, the stakes are particularly high. The Marcos regime is allowing Washington to use the country as a frontline military platform against China while facilitating greater U.S. control over strategic infrastructure, industries, and resources. Under the guise of strengthening national security and attracting investments, these arrangements threaten to deepen the country’s economic dependence, undermine its sovereignty, and expose the Filipino people to the catastrophic consequences of a possible regional war.

Trump’s visit must therefore be met with determined opposition to U.S. imperialist intervention, militarization, and economic domination. The Filipino people must join hands with the peoples of Southeast Asia to resist foreign domination, oppose preparations for war, and assert their right to determine their own political and economic future.

The peoples of Southeast Asia have nothing to gain from being drawn into an escalating confrontation between rival powers. What the region needs is not deeper subordination to competing imperialist agendas, but genuine cooperation based on mutual benefit and respect for national sovereignty and the democratic rights and aspirations of its peoples. (DAA)
